sections.title: Local remediation: Bayes, log-likelihood, and the EM lower bound

keyTerms.definition: p(theta | D) = p(D | theta) p(theta) / p(D).
l(theta) = log p(D | theta).
For any q(z), log p(D | theta) >= E_q[log p(D, z | theta)] - E_q[log q(z)].
Sets q to the posterior p(z | D, theta), making the bound touch the true likelihood.
Maximizes the bound in theta.

recall.question: What does the E-step do?
recall.answer: It sets q to the posterior p(z | D, theta). The bound touches the true likelihood after each E-step, so the likelihood never decreases.

recall.question: What is the observed likelihood with a latent variable z?
recall.answer: p(D | theta) = sum_z p(D, z | theta).

sections.title: Russian-doll ladder for the major mechanism (Bayesian updating)

keyTerms.definition: What was believed before the data; the toy uses Beta(2,2) on a coin bias.
Prior times likelihood, renormalized; the Beta-Binomial update gives Beta(9,5).
The property that makes the posterior Beta(9,5) in closed form.
A point-mass prior that never learns.
The extension tested against a fixed prior on held-out log-loss.

recall.question: What does shell 5 check?
recall.answer: With no data the posterior equals the prior; with infinite data it concentrates at the truth.

recall.question: How do posteriors help in production?
recall.answer: They drive uncertainty-aware ranking; the stakeholder decision is when to abstain.

keyTerms.definition: Sampling for non-conjugate posteriors, named but not implemented here.
Approximate posteriors; the ELBO is stated in U03-C03, full VI is an extension.
Covered as a conceptual link in U03-C07, not the systems.

recall.question: Where is the ELBO stated?
recall.answer: In U03-C03; full variational inference is an extension.

keyTerms.definition: The peak-finder: the parameter that makes the data look most probable, using the data and nothing else.
The gap's noise from n = 10: sqrt(0.7*0.3/10) = 0.145 on the toy.
The MLE converges to the family member closest in KL, not to the truth.

recall.question: What is the MLE on the toy?
recall.answer: p = 0.70 against a truth of 0.65; the gap comes from sample noise.

recall.question: What does the MLE converge to under misspecification?
recall.answer: The member of the family closest in KL, not the truth; e.g. fitting one coin bias to mixture data.

keyTerms.definition: A missing column in the spreadsheet; you sum over its values to get the likelihood of what you saw.
The likelihood of what you saw, after summing over the latent variable.
p(D, z | theta), which EM works with instead of the log of a sum.

recall.question: Why is direct optimization hard?
recall.answer: The log of a sum does not split.

recall.question: When does a latent variable add nothing identifiable?
recall.answer: In a mixture of two Bernoullis observed only through binary outcomes; every start gave -277.0138.

keyTerms.definition: Guesses the labels softly, fits parameters to the soft labels, then re-guesses, each round explaining the data better.
The true likelihood rises each round because the M-step maximizes a bound touching it.
Different starts give different answers; symmetric starts in a symmetric mixture never break symmetry.

recall.question: Why does the likelihood rise monotonically?
recall.answer: The E-step makes the bound touch the true likelihood; the M-step maximizes the bound, so the true likelihood rises too.

recall.question: How do you escape local optima?
recall.answer: Multiple random restarts.

keyTerms.definition: Yesterday's belief as a distribution.
Today's belief: prior times data, renormalized.
The case where Beta prior times Binomial likelihood gives a Beta posterior.
The posterior with mean 0.643 and 90% interval [0.42, 0.83].

recall.question: How does the posterior mean relate to prior and MLE?
recall.answer: Posterior mean 9/14 = 0.643, between the prior mean 0.5 and the MLE 0.70.

recall.question: What does a dogmatic prior do?
recall.answer: A point mass at 0.5 gives a point-mass posterior: no learning ever.

keyTerms.definition: The MLE with the prior pulling toward its center.
The log-prior term; maximizing the log posterior equals maximizing the likelihood minus a penalty.
The MAP moving 0.70 -> 0.67 -> 0.57 -> 0.52 as prior strength grows.

recall.question: How does the MAP move with prior strength?
Is the MAP invariant to reparameterization?
recall.answer: No: the MAP of p is not the transform of the MAP of logit(p).

keyTerms.definition: Averages over every plausible number, weighted by the posterior, keeping the uncertainty.
Plugs one number in, overstating confidence.
The future differing from the past, which makes the predictive distribution honestly wrong.

recall.question: How does the predictive differ from the point prediction?
recall.answer: The point prediction plugs one number in; the predictive averages over every plausible number weighted by the posterior.

recall.question: What are the predictive numbers?
recall.answer: Mean 0.643, 90% interval [0.423, 0.830] from 5000 posterior draws.

keyTerms.definition: Moving toward the data while staying near the start; the pretrained model is the prior.
The quadratic penalty toward the pretrained point, not toward zero.
The prior sd; small tau keeps the model near pretraining, large tau lets the data dominate.

recall.question: What is the posterior mean on the scalar toy?
recall.answer: (0/1 + 2.0/0.25)/(1 + 4) = 1.6, between prior and data, closer to the data.

recall.question: When does the prior hurt?
recall.answer: When pretraining is on the wrong domain; a tight prior keeps code-like biases when finetuning a code model on poetry.

keyTerms.definition: A budget on parameter size; the ridge penalty charges lambda per squared unit of score.
Gaussian MAP; the penalty gradient -lambda s pulls every score toward zero each step.
The penalty strength; the A-B gap falls 5.08 -> 0.48 as lambda goes 0.01 -> 10.

recall.question: What does the lambda path show?
What does too much lambda do?
recall.answer: It kills real signal: at lambda = 10 the gap is 0.48 though the data supports a large gap.

keyTerms.definition: Probabilities meaning what they say; the reliability diagram plots predicted versus empirical.
Binned predictions with each bin's hit rate; the diagonal is the goal.
Sharp gaps pushing predictions toward 0 and 1 faster than reality.

recall.question: What is the mean absolute gap on the toy?
recall.answer: 0.044 across 10 bins, n = 2000.

recall.question: Why does train calibration lie?
recall.answer: The model is calibrated where it overfit; perfect train calibration can pair with terrible test calibration.

keyTerms.definition: Missing completely at random; estimates stay unbiased, only noisier.
Missing not at random, like hard pairs skipped; observed win rates tilt toward decisive outcomes.
Inverse-probability weighting; with true sampling probabilities it recovers 0.899 against the naive 1.077.

recall.question: What happens when hard pairs go missing?
recall.answer: The survivors look easier than reality; the naive log-odds gap is 1.077 versus the full-sample 0.910.

recall.question: When do wrong weights hurt?
recall.answer: IPW with misspecified sampling probabilities can bias more than ignoring the problem.

keyTerms.definition: The world's randomness; the coin still flips, and data never shrinks it.
Our ignorance; the bias might be 0.5 or 0.8, and data shrinks it.
The epistemic part of the predictive variance, 0.016 on the toy.

recall.question: Which uncertainty dominates on the toy?
recall.answer: Aleatoric: 0.218 versus 0.016 epistemic. More data barely helps; better features would.

recall.question: When does the decomposition mislead?
recall.answer: Under misspecification the 'aleatoric' term absorbs model error.

keyTerms.definition: A tournament where each fold takes a turn as the unseen test.
The same annotator's pairs in train and test, inflating accuracy.

recall.question: What are the fold accuracies?
recall.answer: 0.74, 0.61, 0.79, 0.73, 0.65: mean 0.70, sd 0.06. In-sample 0.73 sits inside the fold spread.

recall.question: What breaks with time-ordered data?
recall.answer: Naive shuffling lets the future leak into the past.
